stem: Which enzyme in a biological washing powder breaks down **fat and oil** stains?

options.content: Protease
options.rationale: Protease breaks down proteins, such as egg and blood stains.

options.content: Amylase
options.rationale: Amylase breaks down starch.

options.content: Lipase
options.rationale: Lipase breaks fats and oils down into fatty acids and glycerol.

options.content: Pectinase
options.rationale: Pectinase breaks down pectin in plant cell walls; it is used for fruit juice.

explanation: Lipase digests fats and oils, such as cooking oil and butter, into fatty acids and glycerol, which can be washed away.

stem: A protease in a washing powder breaks down the protein in an egg stain. What are the products?

options.content: Amino acids
options.rationale: Proteins are chains of amino acids.

options.content: Fatty acids and glycerol
options.rationale: These are the products of fat digestion by lipase.

options.content: Glucose
options.rationale: Glucose comes from carbohydrates such as starch.

options.content: Starch
options.rationale: Starch is a carbohydrate, not a product of protein digestion.

explanation: Proteases break the bonds between the amino acids in a protein, producing amino acids and short chains that dissolve and wash away.

stem: Name the type of enzyme in a biological washing powder that removes egg and blood stains.

rejected.feedback: Lipase removes fats and oils. Egg and blood stains are mainly protein, removed by protease.
Amylase removes starch. Egg and blood stains are mainly protein, removed by protease.
Protein is the substance in the stain; the enzyme that digests it is a protease.

explanation: Egg and blood stains are mainly protein. Proteases break the protein down into amino acids and short chains, which dissolve and are rinsed away.
hints: Enzyme names usually end in -ase and are based on their substrate.

stem: True or false: biological washing powders work better in boiling water than at $40^\circ\text{C}$.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not so: boiling water denatures the enzymes in a biological powder, so they stop working. They work best at moderate temperatures, around 30 to 40 °C.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: the enzymes work best at moderate temperatures and are denatured in boiling water.

explanation: The enzymes in biological powders have an optimum temperature of roughly 30 to 40 °C. At much higher temperatures their active sites change shape (they are denatured), so they stop digesting stains.
hints: What happens to enzymes at very high temperatures?

stem: Why does using a biological washing powder save energy?

options.content: The enzymes release heat that warms the water
options.rationale: Enzymes speed up reactions; they do not heat the wash.

options.content: The enzymes remove stains at low temperatures, so less energy is needed to heat the water
options.rationale: Stains come out at 30 to 40 °C instead of in very hot water.

options.content: The clothes do not need rinsing
options.rationale: Clothes washed in biological powder still need rinsing.

options.content: The powder needs no water
options.rationale: All washing powders are used in water.

explanation: Biological powders digest stains at moderate temperatures, so clothes can be washed in cool or warm water, saving the electricity or firewood needed to heat it.

stem: Why does adding pectinase to crushed fruit increase the volume of juice obtained?

options.content: Pectinase turns the fruit's starch into juice
options.rationale: Pectinase acts on pectin, not starch.

options.content: Pectinase adds water to the fruit
options.rationale: Enzymes are catalysts; they do not add water.

options.content: Pectinase kills bacteria in the juice
options.rationale: Pectinase is an enzyme, not an antibacterial substance.

options.content: Pectinase breaks down pectin in the cell walls, so the cells release their juice more easily
options.rationale: The cells come apart and more juice runs out.

explanation: Pectin helps to hold plant cells together. Pectinase breaks it down, so the cell walls break apart more easily and more juice is released; the juice is also clearer.

stem: Lactase is used to make lactose-free milk. What does lactase break lactose down into?

options.content: Glucose and galactose
options.rationale: Lactose is a disaccharide made of these two sugars.

options.content: Amino acids
options.rationale: Amino acids come from proteins.

options.content: Fatty acids and glycerol
options.rationale: These come from fats.

options.content: Maltose
options.rationale: Maltose comes from starch digestion.

explanation: Lactose is milk sugar. Lactase breaks each lactose molecule into one glucose and one galactose molecule. (Cambridge Supplement.)

stem: Match each enzyme in a biological washing powder with the stain it removes best.

right.content: A rust stain from a nail

explanation: Egg is mainly protein (protease), cooking oil is fat (lipase) and sadza is mainly starch (amylase). Rust is iron oxide, which no digestive enzyme breaks down.
hints: Decide what each stain is mainly made of.

stem: The label on a wool jersey says "Do not use biological washing powder". Why?

options.content: Wool is made of fat, which lipase would digest
options.rationale: Wool is a protein fibre, not fat.

options.content: Biological powders only work in very hot water, which shrinks wool
options.rationale: Biological powders work at low temperatures.

options.content: Wool is made of protein, which the protease in the powder could digest, damaging the fibres
options.rationale: Silk is a protein too, for the same reason.

options.content: The enzymes would make the wool change colour
options.rationale: The problem is digestion of the fibres, not colour.

explanation: Wool and silk are made of protein. The proteases in a biological washing powder could digest the fibres, weakening and damaging the garment.
hints: What substance is wool made of?

stem: In an investigation of a biological washing powder, one beaker contains powder solution that has been boiled and then cooled. What is the purpose of this beaker?

options.content: To make the powder dissolve more completely
options.rationale: Dissolving is not the reason; boiling changes the enzymes.

options.content: To show that stains removed faster in the other beakers were removed by the active enzymes
options.rationale: Boiling denatures the enzymes, so any difference is due to their activity.

options.content: To find the optimum temperature of the enzymes
options.rationale: The boiled solution is tested at the same temperature as the others.

options.content: To kill bacteria on the cloth
options.rationale: The aim is to compare active and denatured enzymes, not to sterilise the cloth.

explanation: Boiling denatures the enzymes but leaves the detergent. Comparing this control with the untreated powder shows how much of the stain removal is due to enzyme activity.
hints: What does boiling do to an enzyme?

stem: In a washing-powder investigation, an egg stain disappeared after 20 minutes. Calculate the rate of stain removal, using rate $= \dfrac{1}{\text{time}}$, in $\text{min}^{-1}$.
explanation: Rate $= 1 \div 20 = 0.05\ \text{min}^{-1}$. A shorter time gives a larger rate.
hints: Divide 1 by the time in minutes.

stem: Apple pulp treated with pectinase gave $42\ \text{cm}^3$ of juice. The same mass of pulp treated with boiled pectinase gave $28\ \text{cm}^3$. Calculate the percentage increase in juice volume produced by the active pectinase.
explanation: Increase $= 42 - 28 = 14\ \text{cm}^3$, and $14 \div 28 \times 100 = 50\%$ more juice with active pectinase.
workedSolution:
1. Increase $= 42 - 28 = 14\ \text{cm}^3$
2. Percentage increase $= \dfrac{14}{28} \times 100 = 50\%$ (divide by the control volume)

stem: Complete the sentences about lactose-free milk.

payload.template: The enzyme lactase breaks down {{blank:lactose}}, the sugar in milk, into glucose and {{blank:galactose}}. Lactose-free milk is made for people who are lactose {{blank:intolerant}}.

explanation: Lactase breaks lactose into glucose and galactose. People who make little lactase are lactose intolerant; lactose-free milk lets them drink milk without discomfort. (Cambridge Supplement.)

stem: Lactose-free milk tastes slightly sweeter than ordinary milk. Why?

options.content: Sugar is added to replace the lactose
options.rationale: No sugar is added; the lactose has been split.

options.content: Lactase is a sweet-tasting enzyme
options.rationale: The tiny amount of enzyme does not cause the sweetness.

options.content: Glucose and galactose, made from the lactose, taste sweeter than lactose
options.rationale: Splitting lactose gives two sweeter sugars.

options.content: The milk has lost its protein
options.rationale: Lactase does not affect milk proteins.

explanation: Lactase splits each lactose molecule into glucose and galactose. These simple sugars taste sweeter than lactose, so the milk tastes a little sweeter although no sugar has been added. (Cambridge Supplement.)
hints: Compare the sweetness of the sugars before and after.

stem: A student wants to show that lactase has broken down the lactose in a sample of milk. Which test should she use, and why?

options.content: Benedict's test, because it turns orange-red only when glucose is present
options.rationale: Benedict's test detects all reducing sugars, including lactose itself.

options.content: Iodine solution, because it turns blue-black with lactose
options.rationale: Iodine tests for starch, not lactose.

options.content: The biuret test, because lactase is a protein
options.rationale: This would only show that the enzyme protein is present.

options.content: A glucose test strip, because it detects glucose but not lactose, and lactose is itself a reducing sugar
options.rationale: Glucose appears only after lactose has been broken down.

explanation: Lactose is a reducing sugar, so Benedict's test is positive both before and after lactase acts. A glucose test strip reacts only with glucose, which appears only when lactose has been broken down. (Cambridge Supplement.)
hints: Is lactose itself a reducing sugar?

stem:
Thandeka washed three kinds of stain at $30^\circ\text{C}$ with a biological and a non-biological powder and timed how long each stain took to disappear.

| Stain | Biological powder / min | Non-biological powder / min |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Egg | 12 | 35 |
| Cooking oil | 16 | 31 |
| Mud | 21 | 21 |

Which conclusion is best supported by her results?

options.content: The enzymes in the biological powder had the greatest effect on the egg stain
options.rationale: They saved 23 minutes on egg, 15 minutes on oil and none on mud.

options.content: The biological powder removed every stain faster
options.rationale: The mud stain took 21 minutes with both powders.

options.content: The non-biological powder contains lipase
options.rationale: Non-biological powders contain no enzymes, and the data cannot show this.

options.content: Mud stains are made mainly of protein
options.rationale: If mud were protein, the protease would have removed it faster.

explanation: The biological powder removed egg (protein) $35 - 12 = 23$ minutes faster and oil (fat) $31 - 16 = 15$ minutes faster, but made no difference to mud, which is mainly mineral particles that enzymes cannot digest.
hints: Work out the time saved for each stain.

stem:
Sipho investigated the effect of temperature on a biological washing powder. He timed how long it took for an egg stain on a square of cotton to disappear in powder solution at different temperatures.

| Temperature / °C | 15 | 25 | 35 | 45 | 55 | 65 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time for stain to disappear / min | 30 | 18 | 11 | 9 | 16 | not removed after 40 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: At which temperature did the stain disappear fastest?

options.content: $35^\circ\text{C}$
options.rationale: It took 11 minutes, longer than at 45 °C.

options.content: $45^\circ\text{C}$
options.rationale: The shortest time, 9 minutes, means the fastest rate.

options.content: $55^\circ\text{C}$
options.rationale: It took 16 minutes.

options.content: $65^\circ\text{C}$
options.rationale: The stain was not removed at all.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the rate of stain removal at $35^\circ\text{C}$, using rate $= \dfrac{1}{\text{time}}$. Give your answer in $\text{min}^{-1}$ to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the stain disappeared faster as the temperature increased from $15^\circ\text{C}$ to $45^\circ\text{C}$.

points.description: Enzyme and substrate molecules have more kinetic energy / move faster
So they collide more often and more enzyme-substrate complexes form, so the protein is digested faster

parts.explanation: As the temperature rises the molecules have more kinetic energy, so the protease and the protein in the stain collide more often and the protein is digested faster.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the stain was not removed at $65^\circ\text{C}$.

points.description: The enzymes (proteases) were denatured at the high temperature
The shape of the active site changed, so the substrate (protein) no longer fits / no enzyme-substrate complexes form

parts.explanation: At $65^\circ\text{C}$ the protease was denatured: its active site changed shape, so the protein in the stain could no longer fit and be digested.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State **two** variables that Sipho should have kept the same.

points.description: Any one: concentration / volume of washing-powder solution; size and type of cloth
Any other one: type and amount (volume) of stain; how the beaker was stirred; age (drying time) of the stain

parts.explanation: For example, the concentration of the powder solution and the volume of egg used to make each stain.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Describe a suitable control for this investigation.

points.description: Repeat at each temperature with biological powder solution that has been boiled and cooled (enzymes denatured), or with non-biological powder

parts.explanation: Repeat the experiment at each temperature using powder solution that has been boiled and cooled, so its enzymes are denatured.

explanation: The fastest removal (shortest time) was at $45^\circ\text{C}$. The rate at $35^\circ\text{C}$ is $1 \div 11 = 0.0909... \approx 0.091\ \text{min}^{-1}$. Rising temperature increases collisions up to the optimum; at $65^\circ\text{C}$ the enzymes are denatured. A boiled-powder control shows the effect is due to the enzymes.
workedSolution:
**(a)** $45^\circ\text{C}$ (shortest time).

**(b)** $1 \div 11 = 0.0909... = 0.091\ \text{min}^{-1}$ (2 s.f.).

**(c)** More kinetic energy → more collisions → faster digestion.

**(d)** Enzymes denatured; active site changed shape.

**(e)** Powder concentration and volume; size of cloth; amount of stain; stirring.

**(f)** Boiled (denatured) powder solution, or non-biological powder.
hints: The shortest time means the fastest rate.

stem:
A juice factory in Manicaland tested pectinase on mango pulp. Three beakers each held $50\ \text{g}$ of the same pulp and were kept at $45^\circ\text{C}$ for 25 minutes. The pulp was then filtered for 10 minutes.

| Beaker | Added to the pulp | Volume of juice / cm³ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | $5\ \text{cm}^3$ pectinase | 46 |
| B | $5\ \text{cm}^3$ boiled pectinase | 20 |
| C | $5\ \text{cm}^3$ water | 19 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in juice volume in beaker A compared with beaker B.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why beakers B and C gave almost the same volume of juice.

points.description: Boiling denatured the pectinase (its active site changed shape)
So it could not break down pectin and acted just like adding water

parts.explanation: Boiling denatured the pectinase, so it could no longer break down pectin; beaker B was therefore no different from adding water.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how pectinase increases the yield of juice and makes the juice clearer.

points.description: Pectinase breaks down pectin, which holds plant cells / cell walls together, so cells break open and release more juice
Pectin makes juice cloudy and thick, so breaking it down makes the juice clearer (and it filters faster)

parts.explanation: Pectinase breaks down the pectin that holds the cells together, so more cells break open and release juice; with less pectin the juice is clearer and runs through the filter faster.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which variable was kept the same so that the comparison was fair?

options.content: The mass of mango pulp in each beaker
options.rationale: Each beaker held 50 g of the same pulp.

options.content: The volume of juice collected
options.rationale: This was measured: it is the dependent variable.

options.content: Whether the pectinase was boiled
options.rationale: This was deliberately changed.

options.content: The type of liquid added to the pulp
options.rationale: This was the variable being changed.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest **one** way the factory could improve the investigation.

points.description: Any one: repeat each beaker and calculate a mean / test a range of pectinase volumes or temperatures to find the best / also measure the clarity of the juice

parts.explanation: Repeat each beaker three times and calculate the mean volume of juice.

explanation: Active pectinase gave $46 - 20 = 26\ \text{cm}^3$ more juice than boiled pectinase: $26 \div 20 \times 100 = 130\%$ more. Boiled pectinase was denatured, so it behaved like water. Pectinase breaks down pectin, releasing more juice and making it clearer.
workedSolution:
**(a)** $(46 - 20) \div 20 \times 100 = 130\%$.

**(b)** Boiled enzyme is denatured, so it has no effect, like water.

**(c)** Pectin broken down → cells release juice; less pectin → clearer juice.

**(d)** Mass of pulp.

**(e)** Repeats and means; range of volumes or temperatures; measure clarity.
hints: Divide the extra juice by the volume from the control beaker.

stem: Explain the advantages and the limitations of using enzymes in biological washing powders. [6]

points.description: Proteases digest protein stains (egg, blood) into amino acids and lipases digest fat stains into fatty acids and glycerol (amylases digest starch)
The products are small and soluble, so they wash away
They work at low temperatures (30 to 40 °C), so less energy is needed to heat water
Fabrics and colours are less damaged at low temperatures / the enzymes are biodegradable
Limitation: enzymes are denatured at high temperatures (about 60 °C and above) or extreme pH, so they do not work in a hot wash
Limitation: they can digest protein fibres such as wool and silk / may irritate some people's skin

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Biological washing powders contain proteases, which digest protein stains such as egg and blood into amino acids, and lipases, which digest fat and oil stains into fatty acids and glycerol; many also contain amylases for starch stains. The products are small, soluble molecules that wash away. Because the enzymes work at low temperatures, about 30 to 40 °C, clothes can be washed in cool water, which saves energy and causes less damage to colours and fabrics, and the enzymes are biodegradable.

However, the enzymes are denatured at high temperatures, roughly 60 °C and above, and at extreme pH, so they are useless in a very hot wash. Proteases can digest protein fibres, so the powders must not be used on wool or silk, and some people find that they irritate their skin.

explanation: Advantages come from what the enzymes digest and the low temperatures at which they work; limitations come from denaturation, damage to protein fibres and skin irritation.
hints: Name the enzymes and what they digest before giving advantages and limitations.

stem: Explain why lactose-free milk is produced, describe how lactase is used to make it, and describe how you could show that the lactose in a milk sample has been broken down. [6]

points.description: Some people (lactose-intolerant people) make little or no lactase, so they cannot digest lactose
Undigested lactose is fermented by bacteria in the large intestine, causing wind, bloating, pain or diarrhoea
Lactase is added to milk (or milk is passed over lactase fixed on beads, so the enzyme can be reused)
Lactase breaks lactose down into glucose and galactose, which are absorbed easily / taste sweeter
Test with a glucose test strip: positive (glucose present) after treatment, negative before
Benedict's test is unsuitable because lactose is itself a reducing sugar / use untreated milk as a control

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Many people make little or no lactase, so they cannot digest lactose, the sugar in milk. The undigested lactose passes into the large intestine, where bacteria ferment it, causing wind, bloating, stomach pain and diarrhoea. Lactose-free milk lets these people drink milk comfortably.

To make it, lactase is added to the milk, or the milk is passed over lactase fixed onto beads so that the enzyme can be reused. Lactase breaks each lactose molecule into glucose and galactose, which are easily absorbed and taste slightly sweeter.

To show that the lactose has been broken down, dip a glucose test strip into the treated milk and into untreated milk as a control: only the treated milk contains glucose. Benedict's test is not suitable, because lactose is itself a reducing sugar and gives a positive result before treatment too.

explanation: Lactose intolerance explains the need; lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose; a glucose-specific test (not Benedict's) shows the change. (Cambridge Supplement.)
hints: Why can't Benedict's test tell lactose and glucose apart?

stem: Some cooks wrap tough meat in pawpaw leaves, or cook it with pieces of green pawpaw, to make it tender. Pawpaw contains the enzyme papain. What type of enzyme must papain be?

options.content: A lipase, because meat contains fat
options.rationale: Breaking down fat would not make the meat fibres tender.

options.content: An amylase, because meat contains starch
options.rationale: Meat contains very little starch.

options.content: A pectinase, because meat has cell walls
options.rationale: Animal cells have no cell walls or pectin.

options.content: A protease, because it breaks down the proteins in the meat fibres
options.rationale: Partly digesting the muscle proteins makes the meat softer.

explanation: Meat is muscle, made mostly of protein. Papain is a protease: it partly digests the muscle proteins, so the meat becomes softer.

stem: Which of these is an advantage of using enzymes, rather than other chemical methods, in industrial processes?

options.content: Enzymes work equally well at any temperature
options.rationale: Enzymes have an optimum temperature and are denatured by heat.

options.content: Enzymes are used up in the reaction, so the product is pure
options.rationale: Enzymes are catalysts: they are not used up.

options.content: One enzyme can make many different products from many substrates
options.rationale: Enzymes are specific to one substrate.

options.content: Enzymes work at moderate temperatures and normal pressure, so less energy is needed
options.rationale: Many chemical processes need high temperatures or pressures.

explanation: Enzymes catalyse reactions at moderate temperatures and normal pressure, saving energy. They are specific, so they make few unwanted by-products, and they can be made cheaply by microorganisms; but they are denatured by heat and extremes of pH.
hints: Think about the conditions that enzymes need.
